newsitem.title: USA: U.S. agency EPA poised to strengthen air standards.
newsitem.headline: U.S. agency EPA poised to strengthen air standards.

text.p: The Environmental Protection Agency was expected to propose in the next few days much stricter standards against pollution from smog-forming ozone and tiny airborne particles, health advocates and industry sources said Tuesday.

"These standards would be big improvements over the current standards," said Paul Billings, of the American Lung Association. "Industries are screaming pretty loud, so you know they are an improvement."

Owen Drey, of the National Association of Manufacturers, which is coordinating industrial lobbying against tougher standards, said, "It will affect all industry, but it's not just industry. With that type of change, you're talking dramatic effects to the economy, economic growth and lifestyle changes."
EPA officials said existing standards did not adequately protect public health, but a White House official said the administration recognised that strengthening the standards will have costs.

"The potential economic impacts are not lost on people, and there is a strong determination within the White House to make absolutely certain that EPA plays this straight in terms of giving genuine consideration to no-action alternatives or other alternatives to those that EPA favours," the White House official said.

Industry groups want the EPA to keep current standards, and want that listed as an alternative in its proposal. But health and environmental advocates said thousands of people were dying prematurely and millions were suffering more from lung and heart ailments under existing standards.
While changes were possible before the announcement expected by Monday, industry and health sources said they anticipated the EPA would seek much tighter pollution limits.
A trade newsletter published a Nov. 1 draft of the EPA plan and health advocates and industry sources.

For ozone the EPA was expected to propose reducing the limit to .08 parts per million measured over eight hours, from the current .12 parts per million measured for one hour, health and industry group sources said.
Under the new standard, compliance would be determined by averaging an area's third highest reading over three years, instead of the current standard that allows an area just one exceedence per year.
The agency also was expected to seek comments on alternatives for .07 or .09 standards, sources said.

The EPA was expected to seek new standards for short-term and long-term exposure to tiny particles of less than 2.5 microns in diameter that studies have shown may cause more harm than larger particles because they penetrate lung tissue.

The EPA must gather public comments on its proposals, and is to issue a final ruling in June. While Congress does not have a direct role in the rulemaking, some congressmen have threatened to try to cut off funds to enforce stricter standards or use other measures to block the agency.
